# Part XI: Ecosystem and Economics {#part-ecosystem .unnumbered}

> "A wealth of information creates a poverty of attention."
>
> Herbert A. Simon, ["Designing Organizations for an Information-Rich World"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attention_economy)

The previous parts have shown how models are trained, served, composed,
measured, constrained, and where their limits fall. Part XI asks who can afford
to do those things, who
packages them for everyone else, and how the prices feed back into design. Costs,
licenses, and market structure shape which parts of the technical stack become
common practice.

@sec-model-landscape defines the nouns used to describe a release, including
open weights (weights a team can download and run itself) and the stricter Open
Source AI definition, and reads each release as a set of independent questions:
which artifacts can be obtained, which uses are permitted, what the provider
commits to when it runs the model, and what evidence supports the release's
claims. @sec-model-artifacts follows the downloadable path, where a deployable
model is a versioned bundle of weights, configuration, tokenizer, templates, and
sometimes code. It covers serialization formats and why loading one of them can
execute code, pinning and verifying the exact files fetched from a model hub,
and the data-poisoning and backdoor attacks that a file checksum cannot detect.
@sec-tooling-ecosystem covers the training frameworks, serving runtimes,
gateways, agent hosts, sandboxes, and observability that grew around model
calls, and treats each boundary between two of them as a versioned
compatibility claim to test. @sec-economics then prices the stack: where compute
is bought, why training is a development cost while inference is a recurring
serving cost, when to build a model or buy one through an API, and how to read
historical cost and price claims without extrapolating them.

The second half of the part turns from artifacts to markets. @sec-market-structure
maps the AI value chain from silicon and cloud to model APIs, applications, and
data, and asks which dependency is scarce or hard to replace for a given
workload. Capability and productivity can diverge, and
@sec-adoption-productivity measures productivity as a change in the work an
organization accepts, estimated against what the same work would have cost and
produced under the process the tool replaces. @sec-data-rights-economics treats
permission to use data as a dated decision for one stated use, product, and
jurisdiction. Provenance, legal basis, recorded obligations, technical controls,
and release evidence together determine whether a corpus can become a product
input, and the chapter prices that decision. @sec-agent-economy closes the part
with agents that pay on behalf of a person or organization. It follows one
transaction through authentication, delegated authority, payment, and delivery,
and distinguishes published protocols and pilot experiments from measured
production adoption.

Across the part, the subject is the terms under which capability is made
available: who can obtain it, at what price, under which license, and with what
evidence about its data. Those terms constrain a design alongside the technical
limits described in the earlier parts.
